title: 1.1.1 Definition of economics
definition: Economics is the social science that studies how people, firms and governments allocate scarce resources to satisfy unlimited wants.
overview: The word comes from the Greek for managing a household, and the subject became distinct with Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations (1776). The field exists because wants outrun the means available to meet them, so every society needs some way of deciding what is produced and who gets it. Economists study those choices through four lenses the module names: wealth, welfare, scarcity and growth. The module also notes that no universally accepted definition exists.
highlights: Four definitional lenses: wealth, welfare, scarcity, growth.
Called a "science of choice".
Objective: maximum fulfilment of wants through efficient allocation.

title: 1.1.2 The rationale for studying economics
definition: The rationale for studying economics is that human material wants are unlimited while economic resources are limited, which forces choices on individuals, families and nations.
overview: Because no one can have everything, every decision, from what to buy to how to tax, involves a tradeoff. Economics supplies a framework for judging those tradeoffs by efficiency (using resources well), equity (sharing outcomes fairly) and stability (avoiding sharp swings). It also looks for forms of economic organization that raise living standards or spread wellbeing more fairly.
highlights: Choice sits at the heart of all decisionmaking.
Outcomes are judged by efficiency, equity, and stability.
Economists also look for forms of economic organization that raise living standards or spread wellbeing more fairly.

title: 1.1.3 Microeconomics vs macroeconomics
definition: Microeconomics analyzes individual decisionmaking units and how they interact in specific markets, while macroeconomics analyzes the aggregate behaviour of the whole economy.
overview: The split exists because questions differ in scale: why one price changes is a micro question, while why a country's output, prices or jobs move together is a macro one. Micro uses the demand and supply of particular goods to explain individual prices, outputs and incomes. Macro uses aggregate demand and supply to explain national income, the general price level and employment. The two are complementary, and macro cannot be studied in isolation from micro.
highlights: Micro: individual prices, outputs, and incomes; main tools are demand and supply of particular goods.
Macro: national income, general price level, employment; main tools are aggregate demand and supply.
Newer branches include development, environmental, and welfare economics.

title: 1.1.4 Positive vs normative analysis
definition: Positive economics describes what was, is or will be and can be checked against facts, while normative economics says what ought to be and rests on value judgments.
overview: The distinction exists so that factual disagreements can be separated from disagreements about values. A statement such as inflation is 12 percent can be settled with data, but a statement such as the poor should pay no taxes depends on one's view of fairness. Keeping the two apart helps readers see when an economic claim is a finding and when it is a policy preference.
highlights: "Inflation is 12 percent" is positive; "the poor should pay no taxes" is normative.
Positive disagreements are settled with evidence; normative ones are matters of opinion.
Useful framing for any site section that mixes facts with policy opinion.

title: 1.1.5 Inductive vs deductive reasoning
definition: Inductive reasoning builds general theories from specific observations, while deductive reasoning starts from assumptions or axioms and derives specific conclusions.
overview: A theory is a simplified picture of reality, and economists need systematic ways to build and test such pictures. The inductive route selects a problem, collects and analyzes data, and establishes cause and effect. The deductive route identifies a problem, states assumptions, forms hypotheses and tests them against facts. Both routes aim to produce theories of how economies behave.
highlights: Inductive steps: select a problem, collect and analyze data, establish cause and effect.
Deductive steps: identify the problem, state assumptions, form hypotheses, test them.

title: 1.1.6 Scarcity and economic resources
definition: Scarcity is the permanent imbalance between unlimited wants and the finite means of satisfying them.
overview: It exists because the four factors of production (labour, land, capital and entrepreneurship) are limited while wants keep growing. A free resource, such as sunshine, exists in more than the desired amount at zero price, whereas an economic resource is scarce and has to be rationed. Scarcity is universal and lasting, unlike a shortage, which is a shortterm, specific problem at the going price. It is the reason societies must choose how to use their resources.
highlights: Four factors of production and their rewards: labour (wage), land (rent), capital (interest), entrepreneurship (profit).
Entrepreneurs organize production, make policy decisions, innovate, and bear risk of loss.
Scarcity does not mean shortage.

title: 1.1.7 Choice and opportunity cost
definition: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative sacrificed in order to get one more unit of something.
overview: Scarcity forces choice, and every choice gives up an alternative, so the chain runs from scarcity to limited output, to choice, to opportunity cost. It is measured in goods and services forgone rather than in money, which makes it usable even for options that have no price. When the opportunity cost of an activity rises, people tend to substitute away from it.
highlights: Chain: scarcity → limited output → choice → opportunity cost.
Measured in goods and services forgone, not money.
When an activity's opportunity cost rises, people substitute away from it.

title: 1.1.8 Production possibilities frontier (PPF) and economic growth
definition: The production possibilities frontier (PPF) is a curve showing the combinations of goods a society can produce when it uses all its resources efficiently with given technology.
overview: It exists to show scarcity, choice and opportunity cost in a single picture. Points on the curve are efficient, points inside are attainable but waste resources, and points outside are unattainable. Moving along the curve means producing more of one good by giving up some of another, and the curve is concave because resources are not equally adaptable to every use (the law of increasing opportunity cost). Growth appears as an outward shift, caused by more or better resources or better technology.
highlights: Illustrates scarcity, choice, and opportunity cost in one picture.
Law of increasing opportunity cost makes the PPF concave, because resources are not equally adaptable to every use.
Growth comes from more or better resources, or better technology; gains in one sector alone cause asymmetric growth.

title: 1.1.9 The three basic economic questions
definition: The three basic economic questions are what to produce, how to produce it, and for whom.
overview: Every economy must answer them because resources are scarce. What is the allocation of resources among uses, such as consumer versus capital goods, civil versus military, necessities versus luxuries. How is the choice of technique, labourintensive or capitalintensive, which depends on factor supplies and relative prices. For whom is the distribution of the national product. Economic systems are best understood as different ways of answering these questions.
highlights: What: allocation of resources (consumer vs capital goods, civil vs military, necessities vs luxuries).
How: choice of technique, labourintensive or capitalintensive, depending on factor supplies and relative prices.
For whom: distribution of the national product.

title: 1.1.10 Capitalist (market) economy
definition: A capitalist (market) economy is a system in which the means of production are privately owned, activity is driven by private profit and government intervention is minimal.
overview: It is one answer to the basic economic questions, with the price mechanism answering them instead of a planner. Private property, consumer sovereignty, the profit motive, competition and selfinterest guide what is produced and how. The module credits it with flexibility, entrepreneurship, higher percapita income and capital formation, and faults it for income inequality, unbalanced development, labour exploitation and negative externalities such as pollution.
highlights: Features: private property, consumer sovereignty, profit motive, competition, selfinterest.
Strengths: flexibility, entrepreneurship, higher percapita income, capital formation.
Weaknesses: income inequality, unbalanced development, labour exploitation, negative externalities such as pollution.

title: 1.1.11 Command (socialist) economy
definition: A command (socialist) economy is a system in which the state owns and controls production and distribution, and central planning allocates resources.
overview: It aims to direct resources toward social goals rather than private profit. Collective ownership and a strong government role are meant to give relative income equality, avoid wasteful competition and spread growth across regions. Because there is no automatic price mechanism, planners must make the decisions, and the module points to weak incentives, little economic freedom and red tape as the costs.
highlights: Features: collective ownership, central planning, strong government role, relative income equality.
Strengths: no wasteful competition, balanced regional growth, fewer private monopolies.
Weaknesses: no automatic price mechanism, weak incentives, little economic freedom, red tape.

title: 1.1.12 Mixed economy
definition: A mixed economy is a system in which the public and private sectors coexist.
overview: It exists to combine the benefits of market and command systems. Strategic industries tend to be public while consumer and smallscale industry are private, the price mechanism works in the private sector, and the government regulates essential goods and prices. Governments can use progressive taxation, subsidies and limits on property holdings to promote equality. The risks are inefficiency in both sectors, economic fluctuations, and corruption and black markets if rules are weakly enforced.
highlights: Price mechanism works in the private sector; the government regulates essential goods and prices.
Tools for equality: progressive taxation, subsidies, limits on property holdings.
Risks: inefficiency in both sectors, economic fluctuations, corruption, and black markets if rules are weakly enforced.

title: 1.1.13 Decision-making units and the circular flow model
definition: The circular flow model is a diagram of how households, firms and government exchange resources, goods and money in an economy.
overview: In a closed economy these three are the decisionmakers, and they meet in the product market (goods and services) and the factor market (inputs). Households sell resources and buy goods, and firms buy resources and sell goods, so resources and goods move one way while money moves the other. In the twosector version, household income equals firms' spending on factors and firm revenue equals household consumption. Government provides public goods and can influence households, firms and markets.
highlights: Households sell resources and buy goods; firms buy resources and sell goods.
Twosector model: household income equals firms' spending on factors; firm revenue equals household consumption.
Government provides public goods and can influence households, firms, and markets.

title: 1.1.14 Demand and the law of demand
definition: Demand is desire for a good backed by purchasing power, meaning the buyer must be both willing and able to pay; the law of demand says that, other things equal, quantity demanded rises as price falls.
overview: The concept exists because wants only affect a market when buyers can afford them. Demand can be shown as a schedule, a downwardsloping curve or a function of price, and market demand is the horizontal sum of individual demands. The key assumption is ceteris paribus (other things equal), which lets the curve isolate the effect of price alone.
highlights: Shown as a schedule, a downwardsloping curve, or a function$Q{d}\  = \ f(P)$.
Market demand is the horizontal sum of individual demands.
Ceteris paribus (other things equal) is the key assumption.

title: 1.1.15 Determinants of demand and shifts of the curve
definition: The determinants of demand are the nonprice factors (tastes, income, prices of related goods, expectations and the number of buyers) that shift the whole demand curve.
overview: A price change moves you along a given demand curve, but a change in any other determinant shifts the entire curve. For normal goods demand rises with income, and for inferior goods it falls. A change in the price of a substitute moves demand in the same direction, while a change in the price of a complement moves it the opposite way. The module also notes Giffen goods as an exception to the usual demand pattern.
highlights: Normal goods: demand rises with income. Inferior goods: demand falls with income.
Substitutes: price of one moves demand for the other in the same direction. Complements: opposite direction.
The summary also notes Giffen goods as an exception to the usual demand pattern.

title: 1.1.16 Elasticity of demand
definition: Elasticity of demand is a unitfree measure of how strongly quantity demanded responds to a change in price (price elasticity), income (income elasticity) or another good's price (cross elasticity).
overview: It exists because the law of demand gives only the direction of a response, not its size. It is a ratio of percentage changes. Price elasticity above 1 is elastic (luxurylike), between 0 and 1 is inelastic (necessitylike), and equal to 1 is unitary. How elastic demand is depends on the availability of substitutes, whether the good is a necessity or a luxury, the share of income spent on it, and time, since demand is more elastic in the long run.
highlights: Price elasticity above 1 is elastic (luxurylike); between 0 and 1 is inelastic (necessitylike); equal to 1 is unitary.
Drivers: availability of substitutes, necessity vs luxury, share of income spent, and time (more elastic in the long run).
Cross elasticity is positive for substitutes, negative for complements, and zero for unrelated goods; negative income elasticity marks an inferior good.

title: 1.1.17 Supply and the law of supply
definition: Supply is the quantity of a good producers are willing and able to offer at each price; the law of supply says that, other things equal, quantity supplied rises as price rises.
overview: Higher prices make production more rewarding, which is why sellers offer more. The curve shifts when its determinants change: input prices, technology, prices of related products, taxes and subsidies, expectations and the number of sellers (and weather, for agriculture). Cheaper inputs or better technology shift supply outward, and market supply is the horizontal sum of individual supplies.
highlights: Determinants: input prices, technology, prices of related products, taxes and subsidies, expectations, and number of sellers (weather matters for agriculture).
Cheaper inputs or better technology shift supply outward.
Market supply is the horizontal sum of individual supplies.

title: 1.1.18 Elasticity of supply
definition: Elasticity of supply measures how responsive quantity supplied is to a change in price.
overview: It exists to show how easily producers can expand or cut output when prices move. Supply can be elastic (a small price change causes a large change in output), inelastic, unitary, perfectly elastic (horizontal) or perfectly inelastic (vertical). The module notes that the point method is the one most commonly used to measure it.
highlights: Elastic supply: a small price change causes a large change in output.
The point method is the one most commonly used.

title: 1.1.19 Market equilibrium
definition: Market equilibrium is the price and quantity at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
overview: It matters because it is where the market clears. Above the equilibrium price there is a surplus, which pushes the price down, and below it there is a shortage, which pushes the price up. Higher demand raises both price and quantity, while higher supply lowers price and raises quantity. When demand and supply both increase, quantity clearly rises but the effect on price depends on which shift is larger. The module works through numerical equilibrium examples.
highlights: Higher demand raises both price and quantity; higher supply lowers price and raises quantity.
When demand and supply both change, the effect on quantity is clear but the effect on price depends on which shift is larger.
The module works through numerical equilibrium examples.

title: 1.1.20 Consumer preferences and utility
definition: Utility is the satisfaction a good provides, or its power to satisfy wants, and consumer preferences describe how a consumer ranks bundles of goods.
overview: Consumer theory needs a way to describe choice, so it assumes consumers compare bundles and judge one strictly better, weakly better or equally good (indifferent). Utility is subjective, consumercentred and differs from person to person. Two ways of comparing it are developed in the next concepts: cardinal (measure it in units) and ordinal (only rank it).
highlights: Preference relations: strict preference, weak preference, indifference.
Utility differs from person to person.
Two ways to compare utility: cardinal and ordinal.

title: 1.1.21 Cardinal utility theory and diminishing marginal utility
definition: Cardinal utility theory holds that satisfaction can be measured in units, and the law of diminishing marginal utility says that each additional unit adds less satisfaction than the one before.
overview: Total utility is overall satisfaction and marginal utility is the extra satisfaction from one more unit. The theory exists to explain why people buy less of a good as its price rises: each extra unit is worth less to them. A consumer with one good is in equilibrium where marginal utility equals price, and with several goods where marginal utility per unit of price is equal across goods. It assumes constant marginal utility of money and additive utility, and its limitations are that utility is hard to quantify and the marginal utility of money is not really constant.
highlights: A consumer with one good is in equilibrium where marginal utility equals price; with several goods, where MU/price is equal across goods.
Assumes constant marginal utility of money and additive utility.
Limitations: utility is hard to quantify, and the marginal utility of money is not really constant.

title: 1.1.22 Ordinal utility and indifference curves
definition: Ordinal utility theory holds that satisfaction cannot be measured but can be ranked, and an indifference curve shows all combinations of two goods that give the same satisfaction.
overview: It was developed to avoid the measurement problem of the cardinal approach. A set of indifference curves forms an indifference map, with higher curves preferred. The curves slope downward, are convex to the origin because of a diminishing marginal rate of substitution, and do not intersect, assuming consistent (transitive) preferences.
highlights: Properties: downwardsloping, convex to the origin, higher curves preferred, curves do not intersect.
Convexity reflects a diminishing marginal rate of substitution.
Assumes consistent (transitive) preferences.

title: 1.1.23 Budget line and consumer equilibrium
definition: The budget line shows every combination of two goods a consumer can afford given prices and income, and consumer equilibrium is the affordable bundle that gives the most satisfaction.
overview: It combines what the consumer wants (indifference curves) with what the consumer can afford (the budget line). The consumer maximizes utility where the budget line is tangent to the highest attainable indifference curve. A change in income shifts the line, and a change in a price changes its slope. The ordinal approach avoids the measurement problem of the cardinal approach.
highlights: Combines what the consumer wants (indifference curves) with what they can afford (budget line).
The ordinal approach avoids the measurement problem of the cardinal approach.

title: 1.1.24 Production and the production function
definition: Production is the transformation of inputs into outputs that have exchange value, and the production function is the technical relationship between inputs and the maximum output possible with existing technology.
overview: It exists to describe what a firm can make from what it uses. The inputs are land, labour, capital and entrepreneurial ability. Fixed inputs cannot be changed quickly while variable inputs can, and the short run is the period in which at least one input is fixed, so it is defined by the fixed input and not by a set number of months. A typical shortrun setup holds capital fixed and varies labour.
highlights: Inputs: land, labour, capital, entrepreneurial ability.
Typical shortrun setup: capital fixed, labour variable.
"Short run" is defined by the fixed input, not by a set number of months.

title: 1.1.25 Total, average, and marginal product; the law of variable proportions
definition: Total product is overall output, average product is output per unit of the variable input and marginal product is the extra output from one more unit; the law of variable proportions (diminishing returns) says that beyond some point each added unit of the variable input adds less output.
overview: These measures show how output responds as a firm adds a variable input to a fixed one. Marginal product first rises, peaks and then falls, and it measures the slope of total product. The law assumes technology is fixed, and it explains the shape of the cost curves that follow.
highlights: Marginal product first rises, peaks, then falls; it measures the slope of total product.
The law assumes technology is fixed.

title: 1.1.26 Stages of short-run production
definition: The stages of shortrun production are three regions of the production process, defined by how total, average and marginal product behave as more of the variable input is added.
overview: They exist to show where a firm should operate. In Stage I average product is rising and the fixed input is underused, so it is not efficient. In Stage II marginal product is positive but declining, and this is the efficient region. In Stage III further input additions reduce total output.
highlights: Stage I: average product rising, fixed input underused, not efficient.
Stage II: diminishing marginal returns, the efficient region.
Stage III: further input additions reduce total output.

title: 1.1.27 Types of cost: explicit, implicit, accounting, economic
definition: Explicit costs are outofpocket payments for purchased inputs, implicit costs are the estimated value of selfowned inputs, accounting cost counts only explicit costs and economic cost counts both.
overview: The distinction exists because a firm's true cost includes what its owner's own resources could have earned elsewhere, not just what is paid out. So accounting profit equals revenue minus explicit cost, while economic profit equals revenue minus explicit and implicit cost. Whenever implicit costs are present, accounting profit exceeds economic profit by that amount.
highlights: Accounting profit = revenue − explicit cost; economic profit = revenue − (explicit + implicit cost).
With implicit costs present, accounting profit exceeds economic profit by that amount.

title: 1.1.28 Short-run cost curves
definition: Shortrun cost curves show how a firm's costs change with output, splitting total cost into fixed cost (unavoidable at any output) and variable cost (which rises with output).
overview: From these come the perunit curves: average fixed, average variable, average total and marginal cost. Average variable and average total cost are Ushaped because of the law of variable proportions, marginal cost mirrors marginal product, and average variable cost mirrors average product. A firm can avoid fixed costs only by shutting down.
highlights: Average variable and average total cost are Ushaped because of the law of variable proportions.
Marginal cost mirrors marginal product, and average variable cost mirrors average product.
A firm can avoid fixed costs only by shutting down.

title: 1.1.29 Markets in physical and digital space
definition: A market is any place or digital space where goods, services and ideas are exchanged.
overview: Markets exist to bring buyers and sellers together. The module contrasts physical markets, where buyers and sellers meet in person, with digital channels that carry product value from producer to consumer over networks. Digital marketing uses the internet, mobile phones, display advertising and other digital media.
highlights: Digital marketing uses the internet, mobile phones, display advertising, and other digital media.
Useful bridge to the digital and gig economy concepts in Sources 1.2 and 3.1.

title: 1.1.30 Perfectly competitive market
definition: Perfect competition is a market with so many buyers and sellers that none can influence price, so every firm is a price taker.
overview: It serves as the benchmark against which other market structures are compared. It rests on five assumptions: many buyers and sellers, a homogeneous product, perfect factor mobility, free entry and exit, and perfect market knowledge. The firm maximizes profit where marginal revenue equals marginal cost, and in this market price equals marginal revenue. In the short run a firm can earn economic profit, normal (zero) profit or a loss; the shutdown point is where price equals minimum average variable cost.
highlights: Five assumptions: many buyers and sellers, homogeneous product, perfect factor mobility, free entry and exit, perfect market knowledge.
In the short run a firm can earn economic profit, normal (zero) profit, or a loss.
Shutdown point: price equals minimum average variable cost; the industry is in equilibrium when the market clears.

title: 1.1.31 Monopoly
definition: A monopoly is a market with a single seller, no close substitutes and blocked entry.
overview: Because the monopolist faces the whole downwardsloping market demand, it is a price maker rather than a price taker. Its power comes from barriers to entry, which the module groups into four sources: legal restriction (for example public utilities), control of key raw materials, efficiency and economies of scale (a natural monopoly), and patent rights.
highlights: Barriers to entry are the source of monopoly power.
Four sources: legal restriction (e.g., public utilities), control of key raw materials, efficiency and economies of scale (natural monopoly), and patent rights.

title: 1.1.32 Monopolistic competition
definition: Monopolistic competition is a market structure in which many firms sell differentiated products and entry is easy.
overview: It blends competition and monopoly. The competitive elements are the many firms and the absence of entry barriers; the monopoly element is differentiation (style, brand, quality), which gives each seller limited power over its loyal customers and some control over price within narrow limits. The module separates real from fancied (perceived) differentiation.
highlights: Competitive elements: many firms, no entry barriers.
Monopoly element: differentiated products, so some control over price within narrow limits.
The module separates real from fancied (perceived) differentiation.

title: 1.1.33 Oligopoly and comparing market structures
definition: An oligopoly is a market dominated by a few large firms, each affected by its rivals' price and output decisions.
overview: Interdependence is the defining feature, and entry barriers are considerable. Because firms fear price wars, they lean on nonprice competition such as advertising, warranties and aftersales service. Products may be homogeneous or differentiated, and a twofirm market is a duopoly. The table below compares all four market structures.
highlights: Defining feature is interdependence; entry barriers are considerable; products may be homogeneous or differentiated; a twofirm market is a duopoly.

title: 1.1.34 Goals of macroeconomics
definition: The goals of macroeconomics are the wholeeconomy outcomes policy tries to achieve: full employment, stable prices and sustainable growth.
overview: Macroeconomics studies the economy's aggregate behaviour, covering growth, employment, inflation, income distribution, macro policy and international trade, so performance is judged at the level of the whole economy. Alongside the three main goals, policy also manages budget and balanceofpayments deficits. The ultimate policy objective is sustainable growth and development.
highlights: Performance is judged at the wholeeconomy level.
The ultimate policy objective is sustainable growth and development.

title: 1.1.35 National income accounting: GDP and GNP
definition: Gross domestic product (GDP) is the value of output produced within a country, and gross national product (GNP) adds net factor income from abroad (GNP = GDP + NFI).
overview: National income accounting exists to measure aggregate output and income, using the circular flow idea that one person's spending is another's income. GDP can be measured three ways: the product (valueadded), expenditure and income approaches. If net foreign income is positive, GNP exceeds GDP, and related accounts such as net national product (NNP) subtract depreciation.
highlights: Three ways to measure: product (valueadded), expenditure, and income approaches.
If net foreign income is positive, GNP exceeds GDP.
Related accounts such as net national product (NNP) subtract depreciation.

title: 1.1.36 Nominal vs real GDP
definition: Nominal GDP values a year's output at that year's prices, while real GDP values output at baseyear prices.
overview: The two exist because nominal GDP can rise from higher prices alone, even when output has not grown. Real GDP removes the effect of inflation, so it is the better gauge of actual output growth. The module's worked example shows nominal GDP growing far faster than real GDP when prices rise.
highlights: Real GDP is the better gauge of actual output growth.
The module's worked example shows nominal GDP growing far faster than real GDP when prices rise.

title: 1.1.37 GDP deflator and Consumer Price Index (CPI)
definition: The GDP deflator is nominal GDP divided by real GDP (multiplied by 100), a price measure for all domestically produced goods, and the Consumer Price Index (CPI) tracks the cost of a fixed basket of consumer goods relative to a base year.
overview: Both exist to measure changes in the price level and so to measure inflation. The deflator covers all domestic output, while the CPI covers what consumers buy, including imports. The CPI uses fixed weights, whereas the deflator's weights change as the pattern of output changes.
highlights: Deflator covers all domestic output; CPI covers what consumers buy, including imports.
CPI uses fixed weights; the deflator's weights change as output changes.
Both are used to measure inflation.

title: 1.1.38 The business cycle
definition: The business cycle is the recurring pattern of ups and downs in economic activity around a longterm trend.
overview: It runs through four phases: peak (boom), recession, trough and recovery, and a full cycle runs from one peak to the next or one trough to the next. Cycles vary in duration and intensity. In a boom output grows faster than potential, recessions bring falling output and rising unemployment, and a severe one reaches depression.
highlights: Cycles vary in duration and intensity.
Booms see output growing faster than potential; recessions bring falling output and rising unemployment; a severe one reaches depression.
Fluctuate around a longterm trend path of GDP.

title: 1.1.39 Unemployment
definition: The unemployed are people in the labour force who have no job but are actively searching, and the unemployment rate is the number of unemployed divided by the labour force.
overview: It is tracked because joblessness wastes resources and cuts incomes. The module sorts it into frictional (short transitions between jobs), structural (a mismatch of skills or location) and cyclical (too few vacancies in a downturn) unemployment. The natural rate equals frictional plus structural unemployment, and cyclical unemployment is the part above it. At the natural rate the economy is at full employment.
highlights: Types: frictional (short transitions), structural (skills or location mismatch), cyclical (too few vacancies in a downturn).
Natural rate = frictional + structural; cyclical is the part above it.
At the natural rate the economy is at full employment.

title: 1.1.40 Inflation
definition: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level, measured as the percentage change in a price index such as the CPI.
overview: It matters because it erodes purchasing power. The module sorts causes into demandpull (total demand outpaces supply) and costpush (aggregate supply falls because costs rise). The nominal interest rate equals the real rate plus the inflation rate, so inflation pushes nominal rates up, and its other effects include reduced investment, uncertainty and redistribution of income.
highlights: Demandpull: total demand outpaces supply. Costpush: falling aggregate supply from higher costs.
Nominal interest rate = real rate + inflation rate.
Effects: higher nominal rates, reduced investment, uncertainty, and redistribution of income.

title: 1.1.41 Trade deficit and budget deficit
definition: A budget deficit occurs when government spending exceeds tax revenue, and a trade deficit occurs when imports exceed exports.
overview: A budget deficit is financed by borrowing, and accumulated borrowing is government debt. Through the identity that saving minus investment equals net exports (S  I = NX), a trade deficit means the country is a net borrower in world financial markets. The module's Ethiopian case describes deficits financed mainly by concessional external loans, with nonconcessional loans reserved for stateenterprise projects. For current sourced context on public debt in Jordan and Ethiopia, see Category 5.
highlights: Saving minus investment equals net exports (the trade balance).
The module's Ethiopian case: deficits financed mainly by concessional external loans, with nonconcessional loans reserved for stateenterprise projects.
Useful link to sovereign default (Source 3.1).

title: 1.1.42 Monetary policy
definition: Monetary policy is the control of the money supply, credit and interest rates to steer aggregate demand, usually run by the central bank.
overview: It is a flexible stabilization tool. In a recession it aims to raise demand, and in a boom it offsets inflation pressure. Lower interest rates push firms to borrow and invest more, and higher rates do the reverse, because investment and saving decisions respond to the real interest rate.
highlights: In a recession, it aims to raise demand; in a boom, it offsets inflation pressure.
Lower interest rates push firms to borrow and invest more; higher rates do the reverse.
Investment and saving decisions respond to the real interest rate.

title: 1.1.43 Fiscal policy
definition: Fiscal policy is the use of government spending, taxation and borrowing to influence activity, aggregate demand, output and employment.
overview: It affects both aggregate demand and aggregate supply, with effects in the short and long term. Most governments use it to promote stable growth while also reducing poverty through redistribution. It pairs with monetary policy as the two main macro policy instruments.
highlights: Most governments use it to promote stable growth while also reducing poverty through redistribution.
Effects can be shortterm and longterm.
Pairs with monetary policy as the two main macro policy instruments.
An economy is a web of production and consumption that allocates resources and capital.
Economies nest at three scales (local, national, global) and are increasingly linked by globalisation.
Systems differ by who owns production and how prices are set, and real economies are rarely pure.
Performance depends on growth, unemployment, inflation, interest and exchange rates, and commodity prices; GDP is the headline measure.
The economy shapes living costs, jobs, government spending, and quality of life.

title: 1.2.1 Core vocabulary
definition: The core vocabulary is a fifteenterm glossary of basic economic words that the FutureLearn article builds on.
overview: The terms are boom and bust, budget, capital, debt, economy, economics, financial system, GDP, globalisation, growth, inflation, macroeconomics, microeconomics, recession and stock market. The glossary exists to give beginners a shared language before the article explains how economies work. It notes that debt lets governments, companies and individuals invest beyond what they could afford otherwise, and it defines the stock market as an interconnected system of businesses, investors and securities where shares are traded.
highlights: Good seed for the site's glossary page.
Notes that debt lets governments, companies, and individuals invest beyond what they could afford otherwise.
Defines the stock market as an interconnected system of businesses, investors, and securities where shares are traded.

title: 1.2.2 Local economies
definition: A local economy is the set of interconnected markets and networks within a community, where local businesses, government and residents trade, pay taxes and work.
overview: Historically, production and consumption happened in the same place until around the 19th century. Local economies still exist but are now part of larger networks, linked to national and global ones.
highlights: Local economies still exist but are now part of larger networks.

title: 1.2.3 National economies
definition: A national economy is a countrywide system for distributing scarce resources among competing uses.
overview: Citing the Bank of England, the article describes workers, land and materials as limited while demand is effectively unlimited, which is why such a system is needed. Governments shape their economies very differently (the US versus China is the example given), and each national economy is itself part of a wider network of nations.
highlights: Governments shape their economies very differently (the US vs China is the example).
National economies are themselves parts of a wider network of nations.

title: 1.2.4 The global economy
definition: The global economy is the economy of all humans, covering activity within and between nations.
overview: It includes the exchange of capital and the production and consumption of goods across borders. It is powered by globalisation, international trade, finance and investment, which link national and local economies into one network.
highlights: Globalisation, international trade, finance, and investment power it.

title: 1.2.5 Economic systems: feudalism, capitalism, socialism, communism
definition: Economic systems are the ways societies organize ownership and production; the article describes feudalism, capitalism, socialism and communism.
overview: Feudalism was medieval, with land held by a ruler and allocated to nobles. Capitalism rests on private ownership and the profit motive, with supply and demand setting prices, and describes most economies today (the article's examples are the US, UK and Australia). Socialism means state or public ownership with production by social need (examples given: North Korea and Sri Lanka), and communism means community ownership aiming at a classless society (China, Cuba, Vietnam). The article itself notes countries can be both capitalist and communist, so these labels are simplified and should be verified before publishing.
highlights: Capitalism: supply and demand set prices; the article's examples are the US, UK, and Australia.
Socialism examples given: North Korea and Sri Lanka; communism: China, Cuba, Vietnam.
The article itself notes countries can be both capitalist and communist; these labels are simplified, so verify before publishing.

title: 1.2.6 Market types: command, free, and mixed
definition: Command, free and mixed markets are three ways of classifying an economy by how much the government controls the factors of production.
overview: For each, the article answers what, how and for whom to produce. In a command market, government preferences decide all three. In a free market, consumers decide what, profitseeking producers decide how, and purchasing power decides for whom. A mixed market is a blend, with government setting boundaries for the market.
highlights: Command: government preferences decide all three.
Free: consumers decide what, profitseeking producers decide how, purchasing power decides for whom.
Mixed: a blend, with government setting boundaries for the market.

title: 1.2.7 Other types of economy: green, digital, gig
definition: The green, digital and gig economies are newer types of economy named for what drives them: sustainability, digital technology and shortterm freelance work.
overview: The green economy aims at sustainable development without environmental damage (lowcarbon, resourceefficient, inclusive). The digital economy is based on computers and the internet. The gig economy relies on freelancers and shortterm contracts, which offers flexibility but can make career progression harder. The green economy links to Source 2.1 and the gig economy to Source 3.1.
highlights: The gig economy offers flexibility but can make career progression harder.
Green economy links to Source 2.1; gig economy links to Source 3.1.

title: 1.2.8 How an economy forms
definition: An economy forms when people combine their skills and interests and trade because they expect to be better off.
overview: Citing Investopedia, the article says households, businesses, government, the product market and the resource market form the basic structure, which is the circular flow idea. Trade is the starting point, because each party exchanges only when it expects a gain. This echoes the circular flow model in Source 1.1 (concept 1.1.13).
highlights: Echoes the circular flow model in Source 1.1 (concept 1.1.13).

title: 1.2.9 Macroeconomics and microeconomics
definition: Macroeconomics looks at the big picture of employment, GDP and inflation, while microeconomics looks at how households and businesses make decisions.
overview: Governments set fiscal policy around the macro picture, whereas micro covers individual choices, including the effect of supply and demand. The article stresses that both levels influence how an economy works.
highlights: Both levels influence how an economy works.

title: 1.2.10 Forces and indicators that shape economic performance
definition: The forces and indicators of economic performance are the factors and measures used to judge how well an economy is working.
overview: The article describes an economy as a network of markets of buyers and sellers allocating scarce resources. How it performs depends on growth, unemployment, inflation, interest and exchange rates, and commodity prices, and success is usually measured by GDP. These factors affect income and purchasing power for households and organizations.
highlights: These factors affect income and purchasing power for households and organizations.

title: 1.2.11 How the economy affects everyday life
definition: The economy affects everyday life through four channels: living costs, employment, government spending and quality of life.
overview: Living costs are tied to inflation, booms create jobs, and more tax revenue funds infrastructure and services. Quality of life improves when more resources go to education and healthcare, at least in theory. The article calls its own treatment simplified, so real mechanisms are more complex. A fintech executive quoted in it says tech firms can transform local and global economies through education access and innovative banking.
highlights: A fintech executive quoted in the article says tech firms can transform both local and global economies through education access and innovative banking.
The article calls its treatment simplified; real mechanisms are more complex.
New economic subdisciplines emerge from specialization and the need to adapt to change; advances in physics, biology, mathematics, and technology gave the impetus.
The green economy rests on the idea that nature is neither an endless supply nor an endless dump.
The creative economy rests on creative industries and intellectual property.
The knowledge economy treats knowledge and human capital as the main growth factor and builds on, rather than replaces, economies of scale.
The modern era is defined by rapid change, uncertainty, and sustainability requirements.

title: 2.1.1 Why new economic disciplines emerge
definition: New economic disciplines are hybrid fields, such as environmental economics and green economics, that grow in the gaps between classical specialisms.
overview: The paper argues that sciences have split into narrow specialisms, and the unused noman'sland between classical disciplines became the breeding ground for hybrids like biochemistry. The deeper cause it gives is society's need to keep adapting to change. The drivers it names are modern physics (probability, entropy, information), biology and genetics, mathematics (probability, game theory) and technological development. It cites Drucker on dropping yesterday's problems to free resources for new ones.
highlights: Drivers named: modern physics (probability, entropy, information), biology and genetics, mathematics (probability, game theory), and technological development.
Drucker is cited: organizations must drop yesterday's problems to free resources for new ones, and economics must do the same.
Cybernetics founder Norbert Wiener is cited on fertile research lying between disciplines.

title: 2.1.2 Green (ecological) economy
definition: A green (ecological) economy is, in the UNEP definition the paper cites, an economy that aims at human wellbeing and social justice while reducing environmental impact.
overview: The paper places its rise in the late 20th century, when degradation of the environment became a visible threat to health, safety and jobs. Its core rule is to operate within the carrying capacity of natural resources, because profit pursued at nature's expense eventually backfires. The paper sees the crisis as three interacting problems (resource depletion, climate change and breakdown of the prevailing socioeconomic system) and notes the paradox that the richest regions harm the environment most but hold the fewest people. It describes green economy as still a framework rather than a finished set of answers.
highlights: Core rule: operate within the carrying capacity of natural resources; profit pursued at nature's expense eventually backfires.
Overlapping labels in use: organic economy, green economy, economics of sustainable development.
Crisis seen as three interacting problems: resource depletion, climate change, and breakdown of the prevailing socioeconomic system.
Paradox noted: the richest regions harm the environment most but hold the fewest people; the problem is global.
Green economy is described as still a framework rather than a finished set of answers.

title: 2.1.3 Ordoliberalism and the eco-social market economy
definition: Ordoliberalism, described in the paper as a variant of German social liberalism, favours an optimal mix of market, government and social control over production, distribution and consumption.
overview: The paper holds up Germany's ecosocial market economy as the bestperforming European example of this mix. That claim of best results is the authors' own judgment and is not tested in the paper. The idea connects to the mixedeconomy concept (1.1.12) and to the wider debate over the roles of state and market.
highlights: Links to the mixedeconomy concept (1.1.12) and to the statevsmarket debate.
Claim of "best results" is the authors' judgment, not tested in the paper.

title: 2.1.4 Creative economy
definition: The creative economy is an economy built on creative industries, which produce goods with cultural and symbolic value from imagination, talent and skill.
overview: The concept is old, and what is new is the scale of the link between creativity and economic value. Its scope has widened from music and film to applied arts, software, video games and marketing. It has three elements: the creative person, the economic value created, and legal protection of intellectual property. It creates new, often wellpaid jobs based on skill and talent, and definitions range from creative clusters, to professional occupations and industries, to a holistic view of culture, economy and technology (UNDP 2008).
highlights: Its proponents are often from applied arts and technical fields rather than economics.
Scope has widened from music and film to applied arts, software, video games, and marketing.
Three elements: the creative person, the economic value created, and legal protection of intellectual property.
Creates new, often wellpaid jobs based on skill and talent.
Definitions range from creative clusters, to professional occupations and industries, to a holistic view of culture, economy, and technology (UNDP 2008).

title: 2.1.5 Knowledge economy vs knowledge-based economy
definition: The knowledge economy is an economy in which the management and production of knowledge drive growth, while the knowledgebased economy applies knowledge through technology in products.
overview: The paper presents knowledge as the most important growth potential, driven by information and communication technology, and notes it is often equated with an economy based on human or intellectual capital. It draws on Drucker's distinction between manual workers and knowledge workers. The main difficulty it names is formalizing knowledge and the process of acquiring it, and it says the knowledge economy will not replace economies of scale but will be folded into their development.
highlights: Often equated with an economy based on human or intellectual capital.
Draws on Drucker's distinction between manual workers and knowledge workers.
Multidisciplinary: economists, technologists, computer scientists, and others.
Main difficulty: formalizing knowledge and the process of acquiring it.
Will not replace economies of scale; it is folded into their development.

title: 2.1.6 The entrepreneurial economy and modern-era uncertainty
definition: The entrepreneurial economy is a form of modern economy built around innovation, which the paper says the knowledgebased economy is often identified with.
overview: The paper's conclusion ties its strands together: today's environment changes fast and is highly uncertain, new products reach markets at shorter intervals, and sustainability demands are tightening. The traits it lists for the entrepreneurial economy are innovation, improvement consistent with ecology, factor mobility and sustainabledevelopment requirements, with human capital and management skills playing the key role. It frames the whole modern economy as turning toward nature, creativity and knowledge.
highlights: Entrepreneurial economy traits: innovation, improvement consistent with ecology, factor mobility, sustainabledevelopment requirements.
Human capital and management skills play the key role.
Frames the whole modern economy as turning toward nature, creativity, and knowledge.
Context is the 2022 inflation wave and fear of a global recession.
Central banks raise interest rates to slow price rises, at a cost to borrowers.
Three "warning signal" concepts: recession, the yield curve, bear markets.
Three structural shifts: central bank digital currencies, the gig economy, and moving beyond GDP.
Relies on authoritative definitions (NBER, UK government, ECB, Bank of England data).

title: 3.1.1 Preparing for a new economic reality
definition: The new economic reality is the 2022 setting of high inflation, rising recession risk and widening inequality that the Forum's articles address.
overview: The Forum's September 2022 Chief Economists Outlook rated a global recession as somewhat likely, and the OECD warned that its indicators had worsened. The cost of living was hitting lowincome economies hardest. Forum leadership pointed to growing inequality within and between countries as a legacy of COVID19, war and uncoordinated policy, and the underlying article asks four chief economists how to protect the most vulnerable.
highlights: Forum leadership pointed to growing inequality within and between countries as a legacy of COVID19, war, and uncoordinated policy.
Underlying article asks four chief economists how to protect the most vulnerable.

title: 3.1.2 Rising global interest rates
definition: An interest rate is the price of borrowing money, and rising global interest rates are the response of central banks to fastrising prices.
overview: Central banks raise rates to slow inflation: borrowing becomes more expensive, so households and firms spend and invest less, which cools demand. The cost falls on borrowers, because higher rates push up mortgage and credit card repayments. The topic links directly to inflation (1.1.40) and monetary policy (1.1.42), and it shows the householdlevel impact of macro policy.
highlights: Direct link to inflation (1.1.40) and monetary policy (1.1.42).
Shows the householdlevel impact of macro policy.

title: 3.1.3 What is a recession?
definition: A recession, as the US National Bureau of Economic Research defines it, is a significant decline in economic activity spread across the economy and lasting more than a few months.
overview: The decline is visible in production, employment and real income, and the recession starts at a peak and ends at a trough. Because the definition looks at several indicators over time rather than a single number, it can be compared with the looser businesscycle treatment in the module (1.1.38) and with FutureLearn's negativegrowth glossary entry (1.2.1).
highlights: Compare with the module's looser businesscycle treatment (1.1.38) and FutureLearn's "negative growth" glossary entry (1.2.1).

title: 3.1.4 Foreign currency (forex) reserves
definition: Foreign currency (forex) reserves are cash and other assets, such as gold, held by central banks or institutions like the IMF.
overview: They exist as a buffer. Their roles, per the page, are maintaining liquidity in crises and diversifying a country's financial portfolio. A central bank can also use reserves to support its currency, by selling foreign currency when the home currency is under pressure.
highlights: Roles: maintaining liquidity in crises and diversifying a country's financial portfolio.

title: 3.1.5 Central bank digital currencies (CBDCs)
definition: A central bank digital currency (CBDC) is electronic money issued by a central bank.
overview: The European Central Bank describes it as a riskfree form of money guaranteed by the state, which distinguishes it from private cryptoassets. The page notes that more than 100 countries were exploring CBDCs in 2022, a count that is likely out of date. The topic sits alongside digital markets (1.1.29) and the digital economy (1.2.7).
highlights: Distinct from private cryptoassets because the state backs it.
The 2022 country count is likely out of date.

title: 3.1.6 The gig economy
definition: The gig economy, in the UK government's description, is a labour market in which work is exchanged for money through digital platforms that match providers and customers on shortterm, paypertask terms.
overview: It offers workers freedom and flexibility and gives customers ondemand services. It also raises policy questions about benefits, income security and training. It overlaps with FutureLearn's gigeconomy entry (1.2.7) and connects to unemployment (1.1.39).
highlights: Overlaps with FutureLearn's gigeconomy entry (1.2.7).
Strong candidate for a labourmarkets page on the site.

title: 3.1.7 Beyond GDP
definition: Beyond GDP refers to measures of wellbeing that go beyond gross domestic product, which many economists consider an outdated yardstick.
overview: The page notes that even GDP's inventor, Simon Kuznets, argued for a new measure. The Forum's 2021 postCOVID proposal is a scorecard balancing four dimensions: prosperity, the planet, people and the role of institutions. It is a counterpoint to the module's GDPcentred treatment (1.1.35), since GDP counts output rather than wellbeing.
highlights: Counterpoint to the module's GDPcentred treatment (1.1.35).

title: 3.1.8 Sovereign default
definition: A sovereign default occurs when a government cannot or will not meet some or all of its debt payments.
overview: The page cites 147 governments defaulting since 1960 (Bank of England data). A poor credit rating makes it hard to raise new debt, and credit rating agencies assess a debtor's ability to repay. The topic connects to budget deficits and government debt (1.1.41): borrowing to fund deficits is sustainable only while lenders believe they will be repaid.
highlights: Credit rating agencies assess a debtor's ability to repay.
Connects to budget deficits and government debt (1.1.41).

title: 3.1.9 The yield curve
definition: A yield curve is a graph of the returns investors can expect on bonds that mature at different times.
overview: The page cites Fidelity as saying it can help gauge the economy's direction, and it is read as a picture of bond investors' feelings about risk. It is a financialmarket indicator often discussed alongside recession risk, so it connects to the business cycle (1.1.38).
highlights: A financialmarket indicator often discussed alongside recession risk.

title: 3.1.10 Bear market
definition: A bear market is a market with prolonged price declines, often measured on an index such as the S&P 500.
overview: Bear markets can accompany recessions, and the causes the page mentions range from pandemics to wars. The topic pairs with the stock market definition in 1.2.1 and the stock market concepts in Source 4.2 (4.2.1 and 4.2.12).
highlights: Pair with the stock market definition in 1.2.1 and the stock market concepts in 4.2 (4.2.1, 4.2.12).
Tax practice generally treats as banking whatever the central bank or regulator does, and follows best accounting practice.
Interest payable and bad debts are the special deduction issues.
Baddebt relief follows one of three approaches: commercial accounts, regulatory, or chargeoff.
Trading assets and financial instruments are usually marked to market, with accrual treatment for documented hedges.
International issues dominate for multinational banks: double tax relief, branches vs subsidiaries, transfer pricing.
Turnover taxes on gross income are not seen as best practice.
Data reflects roughly 2002–2004 practice, so it is dated.

title: 4.1.1 What counts as "banking"
definition: Banking, for tax purposes, is whatever the central bank or regulator treats as banking.
overview: Traditional core functions were accepting deposits, honouring cheques, keeping current accounts and lending, with income from the interest margin. Modern banks earn much from fees and trade instruments on their own account, and insurers and others now do banklike business, so tax law rarely defines banking in statute. Retail banks serve many small customers, while wholesale banks (investment and merchant) serve few large ones.
highlights: Retail banks serve many small customers; wholesale banks (investment and merchant) serve few large ones.
Tax treats as banking whatever regulators treat as banking.

title: 4.1.2 Income from assets: interest, discounts, dividends
definition: Income from assets is the interest, discounts, premiums and dividends a bank earns on what it holds.
overview: Interest, discounts and premiums are normally taxed on an accrual basis (when earned, not when received), with marktomarket treatment in some trading cases. Dividends between resident companies are normally not taxed again, except when the shares are held as trading stock, in which case they are taxed as income.
highlights: Accrual: income recognized in the period earned.
Dividends on tradingstock shares are taxed as income.

title: 4.1.3 Gains and losses on realizing assets
definition: Gains and losses on realizing assets arise when a bank sells or otherwise disposes of an asset.
overview: Gains and losses on fixed assets are recognized on realization. Assets held to meet payment demands or for trading are increasingly marked to market, meaning valued by what the asset could be exchanged for between informed, willing parties. Loan novations, assignments, swaps and securitizations can create losses, which are recognized currently if done at arm's length, and stock lending and repurchase agreements (REPOs) are taxed by their substance, not their legal form.
highlights: Mark to market: value by what the asset could be exchanged for between informed, willing parties.
Stock lending and repurchase agreements (REPOs) are taxed by their substance, not their legal form.

title: 4.1.4 Fees and other income
definition: Fee income is what a bank earns for services rather than from lending, such as retail services, custody and advice, capitalmarket work, guarantees and debt factoring.
overview: Fees are recognized when earned and receivable, and fees for multiyear facilities may be spread over time. The rule is the same for commercial accounting and for tax.
highlights: Same rule for commercial accounting and tax.

title: 4.1.5 Interest payable
definition: Interest payable is the interest a bank pays on its deposits and borrowings.
overview: It is normally deductible on an accrual basis. Exceptions apply when the interest looks like a dividend: abovemarket rates, payments tied to profits or limitedrecourse loans. Interest on core regulatory capital (Tier 1, 2, 3) is not deductible in principle, and banks have used offshore vehicles to create capital that is deductible, which links to thin capitalization. Disallowed interest may be taxed like a dividend.
highlights: Interest on core regulatory capital (Tier 1, 2, 3) is not deductible in principle.
Banks have used offshore vehicles to create capital that is deductible; this links to thin capitalization.
Disallowed interest may be taxed like a dividend.

title: 4.1.6 Bad debts and loan-loss provisions
definition: Bad debts and loanloss provisions are amounts set aside, or written off, for loans that are unlikely to be repaid.
overview: Relief for impaired debts is especially important for banks because lending is their core business. Specific provisions (for identified problem loans) are usually relieved, with clawback if the debt is repaid or the provision proves excessive, while general provisions (against possible future problems) get less relief. Three approaches are described: commercial accounts (follow accounting rules, often specific provisions only), regulatory (tie relief to the minimum provisions the regulator requires) and chargeoff (relief only after writeoff, considered too restrictive). Unpaid interest on impaired loans goes to a suspense account and is taxed if later received.
highlights: Commercial accounts approach: follows accounting rules, often specific provisions only.
Regulatory approach: ties relief to the minimum provisions the regulator requires, often disallowing general provisions.
Chargeoff approach: relief only after debts are written off as irrecoverable; considered too restrictive.
Unpaid interest on impaired loans goes to a suspense account and is taxed if later received.
Recapitalization: if public funds cover a bank's losses, the matching tax losses are written off too (no "double dipping").

Table 1.1 examples (c. 2002): general provisions deductible in China (1% domestic, 3% foreigninvested enterprises), Singapore, Japan, Germany, and Italy with limits; not deductible in the UK, Netherlands, Hong Kong, Australia, Korea, New Zealand, or the US.

title: 4.1.7 Derivatives and other financial instruments
definition: Derivatives and other financial instruments are contracts and securities that banks hold for client service, trading, hedging, speculation and as intermediaries.
overview: The usual practice is to mark them to market. The main exception is instruments held to hedge the bank's own risks, which may use accrual treatment if the hedge is documented and the other side is not marked to market. The consistency principle requires both sides of a hedge to be valued the same way, and detailed treatment is left to another chapter of the volume.
highlights: Consistency principle: both sides of a hedge valued the same way.
Detailed treatment is left to another chapter of the volume.

title: 4.1.8 Foreign exchange gains and losses
definition: Foreign exchange gains and losses are the changes in the domesticcurrency value of a bank's foreigncurrency assets and liabilities.
overview: Companies generally keep accounts in domestic currency. Gains and losses on monetary items, which are most of a bank's assets and liabilities, are recognized at the balancesheet date, while fixed and intangible assets are converted at purchase and recognized on disposal. Hedged fixed assets may offset gains and losses so that only the net is taxed, and, rarely, banks working mainly in US dollars may keep tax accounts in foreign currency.
highlights: Hedged fixed assets may offset gains and losses so only the net is taxed.
Rarely, banks working mainly in US dollars may keep tax accounts in foreign currency.

title: 4.1.9 Double tax relief
definition: Double tax relief is a credit or deduction that stops the same income being taxed in two countries.
overview: Banks generally get the same foreign tax credit as other businesses, limited to the tax that would apply domestically, with any excess deductible as a cost. Lending abroad creates a special problem because foreign withholding tax hits gross interest while the bank's profit is only the margin. Some countries cap credit relief on interest (for example at 15%), antiavoidance rules target routing through connected businesses, and tax sparing recognizes foreign tax that the foreign country's incentives spared.
highlights: Some countries cap credit relief on interest (e.g., 15%).
Antiavoidance rules target routing through connected businesses.
"Tax sparing" recognizes foreign tax that was spared by the foreign country's incentives.

title: 4.1.10 Foreign banks, branches, and transfer pricing
definition: Transfer pricing is the setting of prices for transactions between connected parties so that they reflect arm'slength prices, and this section also covers how foreign banks' branches and subsidiaries are taxed.
overview: Double tax agreements and OECD guidelines govern branches and subsidiaries. Interest a branch pays its foreign head office is not normally deductible, except on loans made in ordinary banking business. The OECD splits lending into six components, of which the first four (sourcing, assessing, negotiating, deciding) matter most in assigning profit, while investment banking profits are hard to locate, so a profitsplitting formula may be used. Modern finance moves information and assets across borders at the click of a button, which makes enforcement harder.
highlights: OECD splits lending into six components; the first four (sourcing, assessing, negotiating, deciding) matter most in assigning profit.
Investment banking profits are hard to locate, so a profitsplitting formula may be used.
Modern finance moves information and assets across borders at the click of a button, which makes enforcement harder.

title: 4.1.11 Turnover taxes on financial institutions
definition: A turnover tax on financial institutions is a tax on a bank's gross interest and other income rather than on its net profit.
overview: Some countries use them because they raise revenue without needing to compute net profit. But they ignore ability to pay and hit thinmargin businesses hard, so they are not seen as best practice and are absent from most modern tax systems.
highlights: Not seen as best practice and absent from most modern tax systems.
The stock market includes both primary markets, where companies first issue shares, and secondary markets, where investors trade existing shares.
Public companies in the United States must register with the SEC and make disclosures, including financial statements.
Shares represent fractional ownership; common shares often carry voting rights and may receive dividends.
Exchanges provide organized, regulated trading venues and liquidity; OTC markets involve direct brokerdealer negotiation and generally have less public scrutiny.
Stock prices emerge from buyers' demand meeting sellers' supply, influenced by earnings, profitability, sentiment, interest rates and geopolitical events.
Indexes such as the S&P 500 summarize the performance of groups of companies and serve as benchmarks.
The article's regulatory discussion is U.S.specific: it names the SEC and FINRA.

title: 4.2.1 Stock market
definition: The stock market is the network of exchanges and overthecounter venues where investors buy and sell shares in publicly traded companies.
overview: It is broader than any single exchange: the NYSE and Nasdaq are components of a global system that also includes brokerages and OTC markets. Companies use it to raise capital by issuing shares, while investors use it to buy ownership stakes, receive possible dividends, vote on corporate matters, or sell shares later. The article notes that stock market is often used loosely to mean a particular exchange, but the term covers the whole trading system.
highlights: It connects companies seeking capital with investors seeking ownership opportunities.
It includes exchanges, brokers and overthecounter trading venues.
It supports capital formation, liquidity, price discovery and corporate transparency.

title: 4.2.2 Public company
definition: A public company is a company whose shares can be offered to the general public and traded through public markets.
overview: In the U.S. context described by the source, a company must register with the SEC before selling shares publicly and must comply with disclosure and financialreporting rules. Public status gives a company access to a broad pool of investors, but it also brings reporting and regulatory obligations. The article identifies the IPO (initial public offering, a company's first public sale of shares) as the traditional route to going public and notes SPACs as an alternative route that emerged in the 2020s.
highlights: Public companies must meet listing, disclosure and reporting requirements.
An IPO is a common route through which a private company first offers shares publicly, and it is a primarymarket event.
Public reporting makes company information, including financial statements (see Category 6), more visible to investors.

title: 4.2.3 Share
definition: A share, or stock, is a unit of ownership in a company.
overview: The proportion of a company owned by a shareholder depends on the number of shares issued and the number of shares that person holds. Large public companies may have millions or billions of shares, so one share can represent a very small ownership fraction. Owners may receive part of company profits as dividends and may have voting rights, depending on the share class.
highlights: A share represents an ownership claim, not a loan to the company.
Ownership percentage depends on shares held relative to total shares issued.
Common shares commonly provide voting rights; dividend rights depend on the company and share type.

title: 4.2.4 Primary market
definition: The primary market is where a company first sells newly issued shares to investors.
overview: Buyers in this market purchase shares directly from the issuing company or through intermediaries involved in the offering. The source includes early investors, company insiders and financial underwriters among primarymarket participants. It also includes private placements, in which a company sells shares directly to investors without a public registration process.
highlights: The company receives the proceeds from newly issued shares.
IPOs occur in the primary market.
Private placements are also part of the primary market.

title: 4.2.5 Secondary market
definition: The secondary market is where investors trade existing shares with one another.
overview: After shares have been issued, subsequent purchases and sales generally occur in the secondary market. The issuing company does not receive the money from these later trades; the seller receives payment from the buyer. Exchanges and OTC venues can both host secondarymarket trading.
highlights: Secondarymarket trading transfers ownership between investors.
The company does not receive proceeds from ordinary secondarymarket share sales.
Liquidity depends on the availability of willing buyers and sellers.

title: 4.2.6 Stock exchange
definition: A stock exchange is an organized, regulated venue where securities are bought and sold.
overview: Exchanges are mostly electronic rather than physical places, but they provide a central system for trading and price information. They set listing and trading rules, publish realtime price information and help create liquidity by bringing together many buyers and sellers. Examples named in the article include the NYSE, Nasdaq, London Stock Exchange, Tokyo Stock Exchange and Shanghai Stock Exchange.
highlights: Exchanges provide transparency through price and trading information.
Liquidity is easier when many participants trade the same security.
Exchanges may crosslist shares from other markets.

title: 4.2.7 Over-the-counter market
definition: An overthecounter (OTC) market is a decentralized venue where securities are traded directly through brokers and dealers rather than on a formal exchange.
overview: OTC trading commonly involves smaller or less liquid companies that may not meet exchangelisting requirements. Because public information and trading scrutiny can be lower, investors may find it harder to obtain reliable information. The article describes OTC trading as occurring through broker and dealer networks using computer systems and telephone communication.
highlights: OTC trading is negotiated through brokers and dealers.
It may involve less liquid securities than exchangelisted shares.
Information availability can be more limited than on a major exchange.

title: 4.2.8 Broker
definition: A broker is a licensed intermediary that buys and sells securities for clients.
overview: Brokers connect investors to securities markets and execute trades. Fullservice brokers may provide advice, portfolio management and personalized services, while discount brokers generally offer a lowercost, more selfdirected service. Online platforms have made electronic trading more accessible and often provide research tools and market data.
highlights: Brokers execute buy and sell orders for clients.
Service level and cost differ between fullservice and discount brokers.
In the U.S., brokers are overseen by the SEC and FINRA.

title: 4.2.9 Stock price determination
definition: A stock price is the amount agreed between a buyer and seller for one share.
overview: Prices shown on trading screens arise from the interaction of demand from prospective buyers and supply from existing holders willing to sell, the same supplyanddemand logic as in Source 1.1 (1.1.19). The source identifies fundamental factors, such as earnings and profitability, and technical factors, such as market sentiment and historical price trends. News about profits, interestrate changes and geopolitical events can alter investor confidence and therefore prices.
highlights: A trade requires a buyer and seller to agree on a price.
Higherthanexpected profits may increase demand for shares.
Interest rates and geopolitical events can affect investor confidence.

title: 4.2.10 Market index
definition: A market index is a measure that tracks the performance of a selected group of securities.
overview: Indexes give investors a snapshot of a broad market or a particular sector. The article names the Dow Jones Industrial Average, which includes 30 large public companies, and the S&P 500, which represents the 500 largest U.S. public companies. Indexes are used as benchmarks against which individual stocks or portfolios can be compared.
highlights: An index summarizes the performance of a defined group of securities.
The S&P 500 is a broad U.S. market benchmark; it is U.S.focused and does not represent all global stocks.
Indexes can focus on the whole market or a sector. Detailed index methodology was not verified from S&P Global.

title: 4.2.11 Dividend
definition: A dividend is a distribution of part of a company's profits to shareholders.
overview: Investors may buy shares partly to receive dividend income. The article says ownership can give shareholders a right to part of company profits, often paid as dividends, although payments depend on company decisions and financial capacity. Preferred shares generally provide a set dividend and have priority over common shares in profit distributions or bankruptcy recoveries.
highlights: Dividends are one possible return from owning shares.
Companies decide whether and how much to pay.
Preferred shares commonly have stated dividends and priority over common shares.
Dividends paid reduce retained earnings and appear in the financing section of the cash flow statement (see 6.2.10 and 6.3.4).

title: 4.2.12 Bull and bear markets
definition: A bull market is a period of generally rising prices, and a bear market is a period of generally falling prices.
overview: In the article, rising prices are associated with corporate profitability and economic growth, while declining prices can signal problems ahead. The article does not give a precise percentage threshold for either term. Source 3.1 also defines a bear market (3.1.10) as prolonged price declines, often measured on an index such as the S&P 500.
highlights: Bull markets involve broadly rising prices.
Bear markets involve broadly falling prices.
This source does not give a precise threshold for either term; use a dedicated authoritative source before quoting one.

title: 4.2.13 Investor protection
definition: Investor protection refers to rules and oversight intended to reduce fraud, manipulation and unfair trading practices.
overview: The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission describes a threepart mission: to protect investors, to maintain fair, orderly and efficient markets, and to facilitate capital formation. Investopedia's article describes the SEC as enforcing laws against market manipulation, insider trading and other fraud. These functions explain why public markets rely on disclosure and regulation, including the financial statements covered in Category 6.
highlights: Regulation aims to support fair and orderly markets.
Disclosure helps investors make informed decisions.
The SEC is a U.S. regulator, not a global regulator; Jordan's regulators have not been researched yet.
