title: 5.1.1 Jordan's exchange-rate regime: the dinar peg
definition: A fixed (pegged) exchange rate is a regime in which the central bank keeps its currency at a set value against another currency; Jordan holds the dinar at about 0.709 dinars per US dollar.
overview: The CBJ has kept this fixed dollar rate since 1995, and news reports at the time said it ended speculation about devaluation after the late1980s debt crisis. It works because the central bank stands ready to buy and sell dollars at the fixed rate (a band of 708 to 710 fils per dollar was announced in 1995) and holds large foreigncurrency reserves to back that promise. The CBJ governor has called the peg the best and most appropriate policy for the economy. The tradeoff, raised by commentators, is that Jordan must keep its monetary policy aligned with US conditions even when local conditions differ.
highlights: Fixed rate in place since 1995; a report on the CBJ's 2022 annual report describes an average of 709 fils per dollar (Jordan News).

In November 1995 the CBJ told banks and moneychangers that all dinardollar transactions should stay within 708 to 710 fils; the same package made the dinar convertible for current spending (UPI, 1995).
Reserves were $27.2 billion at the end of May 2026, enough for 9.5 months of imports of goods and services (CBJ statement, Jordan Times); the IMF cites about $27 billion at the end of Q1 2026.
Dollarisation of deposits fell to 18.1% by February 2026 from 18.8% a year earlier, which the CBJ reads as rising confidence in the dinar (Jordan Times).

Commentators note that monetary policy must follow US policy, and that research suggests some autonomy remains because Jordanian rates have not closely followed US rates in the long run (Jordan Times opinion).
Compare with Ethiopia's marketbased birr (5.2.1) and the sidebyside in 5.3.1.

title: 5.1.2 Monetary policy in Jordan: the policy rate and inflation
definition: The policy rate is the main interest rate a central bank sets to steer borrowing costs, and inflation is the sustained rise in the general price level.
overview: The CBJ's Open Market Operations Committee sets the key rate, and it kept it at 5.75% at its 2026 meetings, including the decision reported on 30 July 2026 (check cbj.gov.jo for later decisions). Under a dollar peg, the aim is to keep dinar assets attractive and domestic rates in line with regional and international markets, which supports the peg. Inflation has stayed low: the IMF reports 1.8% for 2025 and projects 2.5% for 2026, and the CBJ cited about 1.9% for January to May 2026.
highlights: The committee's stated aims for holding rates are monetary stability, alignment with regional and international rates, and the attractiveness of dinardenominated assets (Jordan Times, Petra, 2026).
Inflation: 1.88% in the first five months of 2026 against 1.97% a year earlier (Jordan Times); 2.03% for the first half of 2026 (Jordan News). The two reports cover different periods.
IMF projections (June 2026): inflation of 1.8% in 2025, 2.5% in 2026, 2.3% in 2027 and 2.2% in 2028.
The World Bank reports that the CBJ cut policy rates by 75 basis points in 2025.
An earlier statement by the governor said the benchmark rate had been raised by 450 basis points since March 2022 while bank lending rates rose by no more than 119 basis points (Jordan News).
Links: inflation (1.1.40), monetary policy (1.1.42), rising interest rates (3.1.2).

title: 5.1.3 Jordan's growth and its IMF-supported programme
definition: Real GDP growth is the percentage change in an economy's output after removing price changes, and an IMFsupported programme is a loan arrangement that ties financing to agreed reforms.
overview: Jordan's programme under the IMF's Extended Fund Facility was approved on 10 January 2024 (about US$1.2 billion), and a Resilience and Sustainability Facility arrangement of about US$700 million followed in June 2025. IMF reports show growth of 2.5% in 2024, 2.8% in 2025 and 3% year on year in the first half of 2026, with 2.7% projected for 2026 and 3.1% for 2027. The authorities commit to gradual fiscal consolidation, meaning deficits are cut step by step, while protecting priority social and development spending. The IMF notes that the regional war weighs on the outlook, including through energy and tourism.
highlights: IMF staff reached a stafflevel agreement on the sixth review after a mission on 21 October to 3 November 2026; Arab News reports it would open the way for about $294 million. Stafflevel agreements still need IMF Board approval.
In June 2026 the Board completed the fifth review, making about US$134 million (EFF) and US$54 million (RSF) available.
IMF June 2026 table: real GDP growth 2.8% (2025), 2.7% (2026), 3.1% (2027), 3.0% (2028); combined public sector balance 2.8%, 3.0%, 1.6% and 0.5% of GDP.
The IMF links gradual consolidation to the MediumTerm Revenue Strategy and spending efficiency.
Links: GDP (1.1.35), fiscal policy (1.1.43), goals of macroeconomics (1.1.34).

title: 5.1.4 Unemployment in Jordan
definition: The unemployment rate is the number of unemployed people (those without a job who are actively searching) divided by the labour force.
overview: Jordan's Department of Statistics (DoS) reports it quarterly and separately for Jordanians and nonJordanians, because the overall rate mixes two very different groups. In the second quarter of 2026 the overall rate for all residents was 16.1%, the rate for Jordanians was 21.0% and the rate for nonJordanians was 8.2%. Rates are much higher for women than for men, so the textbook types of unemployment (frictional, structural, cyclical, see 1.1.39) are a useful way to think about the pattern, although the releases cited here report rates and not causes.
highlights: Q2 2026: overall 16.1%, down 0.4 points from 16.5% a year earlier; Jordanians 21.0% (21.3% a year earlier); all women 19.9% (DoS, via Jordan News, Arab News and Jordan Times).
Q1 2026: overall 16.1%; Jordanians aged 15 and over 21.1%; Jordanian women 32.7% and Jordanian men 17.9%; nonJordanians 8.7% (DoS, via Petra and Jordan Times).
Net job creation for Jordanians was 87,617 in 2025, the highest figure on record, according to a DoS semiannual report cited by Jordan News.
One economist quoted by Jordan News says further decline depends on the private sector because the public sector can absorb few new workers (an opinion, not a DoS finding).
Check the table before comparing: the DoS reports rates for different groups and age bands (15 and over, 24 and over).
Link: unemployment (1.1.39).

title: 5.1.5 Jordan's public debt and fiscal deficit
definition: Public debt is the total a government owes from past borrowing, and a fiscal (budget) deficit is the gap that opens when spending exceeds revenue in a year.
overview: Jordan's Ministry of Finance reported public debt, excluding holdings by the Social Security Corporation (SSC), of JD 37.38 billion, or 84% of GDP (Government Finance Bulletin, reported July 2026). The government and the IMF aim to bring the ratio to around 80% of GDP by the end of 2028 through gradual consolidation and by reducing the losses of public utilities. The IMF projects the combined public sector deficit at 3.0% of GDP in 2026, narrowing to 0.5% by 2028. Different measures give different ratios, so always check which measure a figure uses.
highlights: The Ministry's methodology excludes SSCheld debt from the official ratio, in line with practice agreed with international agencies (Petra, July 2026).
The IMF's debt measure is the government's direct and guaranteed debt, including the debts of the electricity company NEPCO and the water authority WAJ (footnote to the IMF table).

A news report on November 2025 data put total debt at 108.8% of GDP including SSC holdings of about 25.6% of GDP (Jordan News), and the Ministry's Q1 2026 report presents several measures, including a net figure of 78.4% of GDP. These figures describe the same debt on different bases.
The annual increase in interest payments fell from about 0.95% of GDP in 2024 to about 0.21% in 2025 (public finance bulletin, via Jordan News).
Banks held 51.4% of gross domestic debt (Ministry of Finance, Q1 2026).
Links: budget and trade deficits (1.1.41), sovereign default (3.1.8).

title: 5.1.6 Jordan's external buffers: reserves, remittances and tourism
definition: Foreigncurrency reserves are a central bank's holdings of foreign assets, remittances are money sent home by citizens working abroad, and tourism income is spending by foreign visitors.
overview: These flows bring in the foreign currency Jordan needs to pay for imports and to defend the peg described in 5.1.1. Reserves were $27.2 billion at the end of May 2026, remittances rose 13.3% to $1.6 billion in the first four months of 2026, and tourism income rose 7.6% in 2025 to $7.8 billion. The CBJ and the IMF both describe the external position as strong.
highlights: Reserves cover 9.5 months of imports of goods and services, which the CBJ says is a robust buffer (Jordan Times, 2026).
Remittances from Jordanians working abroad: up 13.3% to $1.6 billion in the first four months of 2026 (CBJ, via Jordan Times).
Tourism income: up 7.6% in 2025 to $7.8 billion (CBJ statement, via Jordan News).
Foreign aid is not covered by the sources used here and remains a gap.
Links: forex reserves (3.1.4), trade deficit (1.1.41).

title: 5.2.1 The birr and Ethiopia's 2024 move to a market-based exchange rate
definition: A marketbased (floating) exchange rate is one set by the supply and demand for foreign currency in the market, rather than fixed or managed by the central bank; the birr (ETB) is Ethiopia's currency.
overview: On 29 July 2024 the NBE issued Directive FXD/01/2024, ending a longmanaged regime (a crawling peg, in the NBE's description) and allowing banks to buy and sell foreign currency at freely negotiated rates. The reform was backed by the IMF and came with a US$3.4 billion Extended Credit Facility. The stated reason was to remove a longstanding distortion: a parallelmarket rate far above the official one had diverted foreign currency away from banks. The effect was immediate, as the official rate moved from about 57.5 birr per dollar on 26 July to 79.4 on 31 July 2024.
highlights: Before the reform the official rate was about 58.6 birr per dollar while the parallelmarket rate was above 115 (East African Review).
Reports describe the firstweek fall as roughly 30%; the rate rose about 38% in birr per dollar, so the size depends on whether you measure the birr's value or the dollar's price in birr.
Other changes in the directive included letting residents open foreigncurrency accounts and removing interestrate ceilings (East African Review).
Commentators at the time warned that a float could bring volatility and inflation, while supporters expected it to restore stability and private activity (Addis Standard oped; AllAfrica).
Source 1.1's birr examples predate this reform, so its birr figures describe the earlier regime.
Links: market equilibrium (1.1.19), forex reserves (3.1.4), the sidebyside in 5.3.1.

title: 5.2.2 The birr since the float: depreciation, intervention and the parallel market
definition: Currency depreciation is a fall in a currency's value against other currencies, central bank intervention is selling foreign currency to ease a shortage, and a parallel market is an informal market that trades at a different rate.
overview: Since the float the birr has kept weakening, reaching a record low of nearly 162 per dollar in midAugust 2026, about 3.2% weaker for the year, while the dollar traded near 180 birr on the streets of Addis Ababa, roughly 15% above the official rate (Bloomberg, via Addis Standard). Demand for dollars outruns supply mainly because of a structural currentaccount deficit and oil imports, so higher global oil prices add pressure. The NBE has sold large amounts of foreign currency to support the birr, about US$2.2 billion this year according to Bloomberg, and at one auction banks asked for four times the amount offered.
highlights: The IMF reports the official rate at 136 birr per dollar at the end of June 2025.
Other reporting cited by Addis Standard puts the NBE's injections since January 2026 at roughly US$3 billion, so figures differ by source and period.

The NBE's reported losses after the reform: about US$2.6 billion equivalent, an operating loss of 428.56 billion birr for the year to 30 June 2025 and negative equity of about 380 billion birr, mostly from revaluing foreigncurrency assets and liabilities (audited statements, as reported by Addis Standard). The same report gives two slightly different foreignexchange loss figures, so check the NBE's statements.
An IMF report in July put reserves at about US$5.9 billion (as cited by Addis Standard).
Forecasts differ: Standard Chartered expected about 163 per dollar by yearend and Citigroup 185 to 195. These are forecasts, not data.
A shortage of dollars at a given price is the same excessdemand picture as in market equilibrium (1.1.19).
Links: determinants of demand (1.1.15), forex reserves (3.1.4), foreign exchange gains and losses (4.1.8).

title: 5.2.3 Inflation and monetary policy in Ethiopia
definition: Headline inflation is the yearonyear rise in the consumer price index, and a monetary policy framework is the set of rules a central bank follows to keep inflation low.
overview: IMF documents report headline inflation of 13.9% year on year in 2024/25, easing to 11.7% in October 2025 as staple food prices fell. The authorities are adopting an interestratebased monetary policy framework with low and stable inflation as its objective, and the IMF has stressed keeping monetary and financial conditions tight. Reports of the IMF's July 2026 review project average inflation of 11.7% in 2025/26 and 12.3% in 2026/27, so the fall in inflation is slowing.
highlights: The IMF's fourth review says inflation continues to decline although the downward momentum is slowing.
The IMF's June 2026 statement says the Middle East war has raised import prices sharply but with only modest effects on output growth and inflation so far.
Addis Insight reports a projected 55.9% rise in credit to the private sector and stateowned enterprises in 2025/26, which the IMF said needs close monitoring (secondary report).
Links: inflation (1.1.40), monetary policy (1.1.42), rising interest rates (3.1.2).

title: 5.2.4 Ethiopia's IMF programme, growth and debt restructuring
definition: Debt restructuring is an agreement with creditors to change the terms of existing loans, for example by extending maturities or lowering payments, so that a borrower can keep servicing them.
overview: Ethiopia's fouryear US$3.4 billion Extended Credit Facility was approved in July 2024 alongside the exchangerate reform. By the fifth review, completed around July 2026 with about US$464 million released, total drawings were about US$2.65 billion (Addis Insight). IMF documents describe strong growth and reserves accumulation but also a Middle East conflict that creates financing pressure. Growth is projected at 9.2% in 2025/26, slowing to 7.8% in 2026/27 (reports of the IMF's July 2026 review and October 2026 outlook). Ethiopia has been restructuring external debt under the G20 Common Framework and reached an agreement with its Official Creditor Committee on about US$3.5 billion in loans (Bloomberg, via Addis Standard).
highlights: Source 1.1 (1.1.41) describes deficits financed mainly by concessional external loans; this concept gives the current debt picture.
The fifth review's stafflevel agreement was announced on 3 June 2026 for about US$468 million; Addis Insight reports a completed review with about US$464 million, so amounts differ by report.
Ethiopia's figures are for fiscal years, so growth of 9.2% for 2026 refers to the year ending mid2026.
Bloomberg, as reported by Addis Standard, links the birr's outlook to progress on the debt restructuring.
Links: budget and trade deficits (1.1.41), sovereign default (3.1.8), GDP (1.1.35).
A peg buys predictability at the price of independent monetary policy.
A float lets the currency absorb shocks but exposes it to market pressure.

title: 5.3.1 Fixed vs market-based exchange rates: Jordan and Ethiopia side by side
definition: A fixed exchange rate holds a currency at a set value against an anchor currency, while a marketbased (floating) rate lets supply and demand decide its value.
overview: Jordan has held the dinar at about 0.709 per US dollar since 1995, defending it with reserves and interest rates aligned to the dollar, and gains stable prices and predictable trade costs at the cost of independent monetary policy. Ethiopia moved the other way in July 2024: the birr is now set by banks' negotiated rates, which narrowed the gap with the parallel market but let the currency fall from about 57 to over 160 per dollar and exposed the central bank to large revaluation losses. The comparison shows the core tradeoff between stability under a peg and flexibility, with exposure to market pressure, under a float.
highlights: Rate: dinar fixed near 0.709 per dollar (CBJ); birr marketbased, from about 57 per dollar in June 2024 to about 136 in June 2025 and nearly 162 in August 2026.
Inflation: Jordan about 1.8% to 2.5% (IMF, CBJ); Ethiopia 11.7% to 13.9% in the periods quoted (IMF).
Reserves: Jordan about $27 billion (about 9.5 months of imports, CBJ); Ethiopia about $5.9 billion (an IMF estimate cited by Addis Standard). The measures differ, so compare with care.
Parallel market: the sources used here report none for Jordan; Ethiopia's was about 15% above the official rate in August 2026.

Teaching link (editorial): a fixed rate behaves like a price set by the central bank, which must buy or sell foreign currency to make it hold. A shortage of dollars at a fixed price is the excessdemand picture from market equilibrium (1.1.19), and the supply and demand widget on that page can be used to illustrate it.
Links: monetary policy (1.1.42), forex reserves (3.1.4), the dinar peg (5.1.1), the birr float (5.2.1, 5.2.2).
The income statement measures profitability over a period, such as a month, quarter or year.
Revenue minus cost of goods sold equals gross profit.
Operating expenses are deducted from gross profit to obtain operating income.
Interest, other items and income taxes are then considered before net income.
Net income divided by weighted average shares outstanding gives earnings per share.
Depreciation and amortization are noncash expenses that spread the cost of longlived assets over time.

title: 6.1.1 Income statement
definition: The income statement reports a company's revenues, expenses and resulting profit or loss for a period.
overview: It is also called a profit and loss statement, or P&L, although CFI notes that the terms are often used interchangeably. It covers a time period rather than a single date and helps users assess whether operations generated a profit. It is one of the three core financial statements and is commonly the starting point for financial models.
highlights: It covers a period, not a point in time.
It shows profitability from operating and nonoperating activities.
It is also called a P&L.

title: 6.1.2 Revenue
definition: Revenue is the income a company earns from selling goods or providing services.
overview: Revenue appears at the top of the income statement and is sometimes called sales or the top line. A company may have several revenue streams, such as product sales and service fees, which combine into total revenue. Revenue is recorded before deducting the costs of producing or delivering the related goods and services.
highlights: Revenue is the starting point of the income statement.
It may come from multiple products or services.
It is measured before direct costs are deducted.

title: 6.1.3 Cost of goods sold
definition: Cost of goods sold, or COGS, includes the direct costs of producing goods sold or delivering services.
overview: CFI says the line may also be called cost of sales, especially for service businesses. Direct costs can include labor, parts, materials and an allocated share of expenses such as depreciation. COGS is subtracted from revenue to calculate gross profit.
highlights: COGS includes direct production or servicedelivery costs.
It may be labelled cost of sales.
It is deducted from revenue to obtain gross profit.

title: 6.1.4 Gross profit
definition: Gross profit is revenue minus cost of goods sold.
overview: It shows the profit remaining after direct costs but before operating expenses, interest and taxes. CFI identifies gross profit as a key subtotal and notes that analysts often compare it with total sales to calculate gross profit margin. A higher gross profit does not by itself mean high overall profitability, because operating and financing costs still need to be paid.
highlights: Gross profit = Revenue  COGS.
It excludes operating expenses, interest and taxes.
Gross margin compares gross profit with revenue.

title: 6.1.5 Operating expenses
definition: Operating expenses are the indirect costs of running the business.
overview: CFI groups selling, general and administrative expenses under this broad category. Examples include salaries and wages, rent, office expenses, insurance, travel, and sometimes depreciation and amortization (noncash charges that spread the cost of longlived assets over time). These expenses are deducted from gross profit to arrive at operating income.
highlights: Operating expenses support the business but are not direct production costs.
SG&A is a common label for selling, general and administrative expenses.
They are deducted before operating income is calculated.

title: 6.1.6 Operating income
definition: Operating income is profit from regular business operations before interest and taxes.
overview: CFI also calls it EBIT, meaning earnings before interest and taxes. It is calculated after revenue, COGS and operating expenses, but before nonoperating income or expense, interest and taxes. It helps users see whether the core business is profitable independently of financing costs and tax effects.
highlights: Operating income = Gross profit  Operating expenses.
It is also called EBIT.
It excludes interest and income taxes.

title: 6.1.7 Interest expense
definition: Interest expense is the cost a company pays for borrowed money.
overview: CFI says companies commonly show interest expense and interest income separately to reconcile the difference between EBIT and earnings before tax. Interest expense is linked to a company's debt schedule. It is deducted after operating income in the income statement.
highlights: Interest expense reflects the cost of debt.
It is separate from operating income.
It reduces pretax income.

title: 6.1.8 Income taxes
definition: Income taxes are taxes charged on a company's pretax income.
overview: CFI states that income taxes are deducted from pretax income to arrive at net income. The tax expense can include both current taxes and future taxes. Tax rules and rates differ by jurisdiction, so the same pretax profit can produce different tax expenses in different countries.
highlights: Income taxes are deducted after pretax income.
Tax expense may include current and deferred components.
Tax treatment varies by jurisdiction.

title: 6.1.9 Net income
definition: Net income is a company's profit after all expenses, interest and taxes.
overview: It is the bottom line of the income statement and can be a net profit or net loss. CFI explains that net income flows into retained earnings on the balance sheet, after any dividends are considered. It is also the usual starting point for the indirect method of preparing operating cash flow.
highlights: Net income = Pretax income  Income taxes.
It is the income statement's bottom line.
It links to retained earnings and operating cash flow.

title: 6.1.10 Earnings per share
definition: Earnings per share, or EPS, is net income divided by weighted average shares outstanding.
overview: EPS expresses profit on a pershare basis, making it easier to compare results across periods or companies with different numbers of shares. It is a reported measure, not a measure of cash available to the company. It connects the income statement to the stock market concepts in Source 4.2.
highlights: EPS = Net income / Weighted average shares outstanding.
It standardizes profit per share.
It does not itself show cash flow.

title: 6.1.11 Single-step and multi-step formats
definition: A singlestep income statement subtracts total expenses from total revenues in one calculation, while a multistep format presents subtotals such as gross profit and operating income.
overview: CFI's explanation follows a multistep structure, separating COGS, gross profit, operating expenses, operating income, interest, taxes and net income. A singlestep format is simpler because it groups revenues and expenses before calculating net income. The choice of format affects presentation, not the underlying economic events.
highlights: Multistep statements show intermediate profit subtotals.
Singlestep statements use a simpler revenueminusexpense structure.
Both formats aim to arrive at net income.

title: 6.1.12 Accrual accounting
definition: Accrual accounting records revenues and expenses when they are earned or incurred, rather than only when cash moves.
overview: CFI says the income statement uses accounting principles including matching and accruals, rather than presenting figures on a cash basis. This means a sale made on credit can increase revenue and accounts receivable before cash is received. It also means expenses can be recognized before the related cash is paid.
highlights: Revenue may be recognized before cash is received.
Expenses may be recognized before cash is paid.
This is why net income can differ from operating cash flow.
The balance sheet is a snapshot at a particular date.
Assets equal liabilities plus shareholders' equity.
Current items are expected to convert to cash or become due within one year; noncurrent items extend beyond one year.
Assets are commonly ordered from most liquid to least liquid.
Retained earnings accumulate net income kept in the business after dividends.
The balance sheet supports liquidity, leverage, efficiency and return ratios.

title: 6.2.1 Balance sheet
definition: The balance sheet reports a company's assets, liabilities and equity at a specific point in time.
overview: It is also called the statement of financial position. It provides a snapshot rather than a period measure, showing the resources a company controls, the claims of creditors and the residual interest of owners. It is used to assess financial strength, liquidity and capital structure.
highlights: It is a pointintime statement.
It has three main sections: assets, liabilities and equity.
It is also called the statement of financial position.

title: 6.2.2 Accounting equation
definition: The accounting equation states that assets equal liabilities plus equity.
overview: CFI presents this as the structure underlying the balance sheet. Assets are resources the business owns or controls; liabilities are obligations owed to others; equity is the residual interest remaining for owners after liabilities are deducted. The equation must hold for the balance sheet to balance.
highlights: Assets = Liabilities + Equity.
Equity can also be viewed as assets minus liabilities.
A change on one side must be matched elsewhere for the equation to hold.

title: 6.2.3 Assets
definition: Assets are resources a company owns or controls that are expected to provide future economic benefit.
overview: CFI lists cash, inventory, property and equipment as examples. Assets are divided into current and noncurrent categories. Their balancesheet value may differ from their current market value, particularly for longlived assets recorded net of accumulated depreciation.
highlights: Assets represent resources controlled by the company.
They include cash, receivables, inventory and fixed assets.
They are classified by expected conversion or use period.

title: 6.2.4 Current assets
definition: Current assets are assets expected to be converted into cash, sold or used within one year.
overview: CFI places cash and equivalents first, followed by accounts receivable and inventory. These assets support shortterm operations and are relevant to liquidity analysis. The classification can depend on the company's operating cycle where that cycle is longer than one year.
highlights: Cash and equivalents are the most liquid current assets.
Accounts receivable represents credit sales not yet collected.
Inventory includes raw materials, work in progress and finished goods.

title: 6.2.5 Non-current assets
definition: Noncurrent assets are assets held for more than one year.
overview: CFI includes property, plant and equipment (PP&E) and intangible assets in this category. PP&E is reported net of accumulated depreciation, while land is not depreciated. Intangible assets can include identifiable items such as patents and licences, as well as unidentifiable items such as goodwill.
highlights: PP&E is tangible, longlived operating property.
Depreciation reduces the reported carrying amount of depreciable PP&E.
Intangible assets include items such as patents, licences and goodwill.

title: 6.2.6 Liabilities
definition: Liabilities are obligations a company owes to other parties.
overview: CFI gives loans and accounts payable as examples. Liabilities are divided into current liabilities, due within one year, and noncurrent liabilities, due later. They represent claims on the company's assets before shareholders' residual claim.
highlights: Liabilities are obligations to external parties.
They include trade payables and borrowings.
They are classified by expected payment timing.

title: 6.2.7 Current liabilities
definition: Current liabilities are obligations due within one year or within the company's operating cycle, if longer.
overview: CFI includes accounts payable, current debt or notes payable, and the current portion of longterm debt. Accounts payable represents amounts owed to suppliers for credit purchases. The current portion of longterm debt is the part of a longer loan that must be repaid in the coming year.
highlights: Accounts payable arises from purchases on credit.
Current debt must be repaid within the short term.
Part of longterm debt can become a current liability as repayment approaches.

title: 6.2.8 Non-current liabilities
definition: Noncurrent liabilities are obligations due after more than one year.
overview: CFI includes bonds payable and longterm debt in this group. Longterm debt excludes the portion classified as current. These obligations affect a company's leverage and future cash commitments.
highlights: Longterm debt matures beyond one year.
Bonds payable are a form of longterm borrowing.
They affect leverage and future financing needs.

title: 6.2.9 Equity
definition: Equity is the owners' residual interest in the company after liabilities are deducted from assets.
overview: CFI identifies share capital and retained earnings as major equity components. Share capital represents funds invested by shareholders, while retained earnings represent accumulated net income kept in the company. Dividends reduce retained earnings when paid.
highlights: Equity = Assets  Liabilities.
Share capital reflects owner investment.
Retained earnings reflect accumulated profit kept in the business.

title: 6.2.10 Retained earnings
definition: Retained earnings are cumulative net income kept by the company rather than distributed as dividends.
overview: CFI explains that each period's net income may increase retained earnings, while dividends reduce them. Retained earnings can therefore become negative if accumulated losses or distributions exceed prior retained profits. The account links the income statement to the balance sheet.
highlights: Retained earnings increase with net income kept in the business.
Dividends reduce retained earnings.
They connect current and priorperiod income statements to equity.

title: 6.2.11 Liquidity ordering
definition: Liquidity ordering places more easily convertible assets first on the balance sheet.
overview: CFI says cash, inventory and trade payables are placed in the current section before less liquid items such as PP&E and longterm debt. This presentation helps readers quickly see resources available in the short term and obligations due soon. The exact ordering can vary by company and reporting framework.
highlights: Cash is usually shown first among assets.
Current items precede noncurrent items.
Ordering highlights shortterm resources and obligations.

title: 6.2.12 Current ratio and debt-to-equity ratio
definition: The current ratio compares current assets with current liabilities, and debttoequity compares debt with shareholders' equity.
overview: CFI classifies the current ratio as a liquidity ratio and debttoequity as a leverage ratio. The current ratio indicates whether shortterm assets appear sufficient to cover shortterm obligations. Debttoequity indicates the extent to which the company relies on borrowing relative to owners' equity.
highlights: Current ratio = Current assets / Current liabilities.
Debttoequity compares debt with equity.
Ratios support comparison, but must be interpreted in context.
The statement covers a period and shows cash inflows and outflows.
Operating activities relate to the principal revenueproducing activities of the business.
Investing activities include buying and selling longterm assets and investments.
Financing activities include borrowing, repaying debt, issuing or repurchasing shares and paying dividends.
The indirect method begins with profit and adjusts for noncash items and workingcapital changes.
The ending cash balance must equal the cash balance reported on the balance sheet.

title: 6.3.1 Cash flow statement
definition: The cash flow statement reports cash received and cash paid during a period.
overview: It shows how a company generated and used cash across operating, investing and financing activities. It bridges the income statement and balance sheet by explaining why the cash balance changed. It is particularly useful for assessing liquidity and whether reported earnings are supported by cash generation.
highlights: It covers a period, not a single date.
It tracks cash and cash equivalents.
It explains the change in the cash balance.

title: 6.3.2 Operating activities
definition: Operating activities are the principal revenueproducing activities of a business, plus other activities that are neither investing nor financing activities.
overview: This section includes cash from sales and cash paid for operating costs such as rent, salaries and administration. Under the indirect method, it begins with net income and adjusts for noncash expenses and workingcapital movements. It is the section most directly connected with daytoday business operations.
highlights: It includes cash from sales and operating payments.
It is adjusted for noncash items under the indirect method.
It can be compared with net income to assess earnings quality.

title: 6.3.3 Investing activities
definition: Investing activities are cash flows from acquiring or disposing of longterm assets and other investments not classified as cash equivalents.
overview: CFI includes purchases and sales of property, plant and equipment, other noncurrent assets and financial assets. Cash spent on PP&E is called capital expenditure, or CapEx, and is a cash outflow. Selling such assets generates a cash inflow.
highlights: CapEx is cash spent on longlived operating assets.
Asset sales produce investing cash inflows.
This section concerns longterm resources, not daily operating payments.

title: 6.3.4 Financing activities
definition: Financing activities are cash flows arising from changes in a company's capital structure.
overview: CFI includes borrowing and repaying loans or bonds, issuing or buying back shares, and paying dividends. Debt issuance and equity issuance bring cash into the company, while repayments, buybacks and dividends use cash. This section shows how the company funds itself and returns capital to providers of finance.
highlights: Debt issuance is a cash inflow; repayment is an outflow.
Share issuance is a cash inflow; buybacks are an outflow.
Dividends paid are financing outflows in the usual presentation (IFRS allows a choice, see 6.4).

title: 6.3.5 Direct method
definition: The direct method presents major classes of gross cash receipts and gross cash payments from operating activities.
overview: CFI describes it as a straightforward presentation of cash received from customers and cash paid for operating expenses. It is less commonly used than the indirect method. It gives a more immediate view of operating cash receipts and payments, but it requires more detailed cashtransaction information.
highlights: It lists major operating cash receipts and payments.
It shows cash flows directly rather than reconciling from profit.
It is less commonly used than the indirect method.

title: 6.3.6 Indirect method
definition: The indirect method starts with profit and adjusts it for noncash items, accruals, deferrals, and investing or financingrelated income and expenses.
overview: CFI says most companies use this method. Depreciation and amortization are added back because they reduced profit without requiring cash payment. Changes in receivables, inventory and payables are then adjusted to reflect the timing difference between accounting recognition and cash movement.
highlights: It reconciles profit to operating cash flow.
Depreciation and amortization are added back.
Workingcapital changes adjust for cashtiming differences.

title: 6.3.7 Depreciation add-back
definition: A depreciation addback reverses the effect of depreciation expense when calculating operating cash flow under the indirect method.
overview: Depreciation spreads the cost of a tangible longlived asset over its useful life and reduces net income, but it does not itself require a cash payment. Amortization does the same for certain intangible assets. Adding these expenses back prevents them from being treated as cash outflows in the operating section.
highlights: Depreciation reduces accounting profit but not cash directly.
It is added back in the indirect operating section.
The related cash outflow occurs when the asset is purchased, usually in investing activities.

title: 6.3.8 Working-capital changes
definition: Workingcapital changes are movements in current assets other than cash and current liabilities other than debt that affect operating cash flow.
overview: CFI explains that an increase in inventory or accounts receivable reduces operating cash flow because cash is tied up or not yet collected. An increase in accounts payable increases operating cash flow because the company has not yet paid suppliers. These adjustments convert accrualbased profit into cashbased operating performance.
highlights: Higher receivables or inventory generally reduce operating cash flow.
Higher payables generally increase operating cash flow.
Working capital links the balance sheet to operating cash flow.

title: 6.3.9 Net income is not cash
definition: Net income is accounting profit under accrual rules, while cash flow is the actual movement of cash and cash equivalents.
overview: CFI emphasizes that incomestatement and balancesheet figures are accrualbased, so they do not directly measure cash movement. A company can report positive net income while cash flow is lower because sales were made on credit, inventory increased or expenses were accrued. The cash flow statement adjusts for these timing and noncash differences.
highlights: Net income can include noncash revenue or expenses.
Credit sales increase revenue before cash is received.
The cash flow statement reconciles profit with actual cash movement.

title: 6.3.10 Free cash flow
definition: Free cash flow is cash generated by operations after investment in longlived operating assets.
overview: CFI identifies capital expenditure as the main investing outflow for many companies. A common practical calculation is operating cash flow minus capital expenditure. It indicates cash available after maintaining or expanding the asset base, before considering financing decisions.
highlights: Free cash flow = Operating cash flow  Capital expenditure.
It focuses on cash after investment in productive assets.
It is not a line item required on the face of the cash flow statement, and definitions vary in practice.

title: 6.3.11 Ending cash balance
definition: The ending cash balance is the cash and cashequivalent balance at the end of the reporting period.
overview: CFI explains that the net change in cash from operating, investing and financing activities is added to the opening cash balance to derive the closing balance. That closing balance is reported in current assets on the balance sheet. This is a central check when linking the three statements.
highlights: Ending cash = Beginning cash + Net change in cash.
Net change in cash = CFO + CFI + CFF.
Ending cash must match balancesheet cash.
IAS 7 requires a statement of cash flows for each period for which financial statements are presented.
Cash flows must be classified into operating, investing and financing activities.
Either the direct or indirect method may be used for operating cash flows.
Cash includes cash on hand and demand deposits; cash equivalents are shortterm, highly liquid investments with insignificant valuechange risk.
Noncash investing and financing transactions are excluded from the statement but separately disclosed.
The standard requires reconciliation between cash and cash equivalents in the cash flow statement and the equivalent balancesheet items.

title: 6.4.1 Cash and cash equivalents
definition: Cash includes cash on hand and demand deposits, and cash equivalents are shortterm, highly liquid investments readily convertible to known cash amounts with insignificant valuechange risk.
overview: IAS 7 uses this definition to determine what belongs in the cash flow statement. The distinction matters because not every liquid asset qualifies as a cash equivalent. The standard requires disclosure of the components of cash and cash equivalents.
highlights: Cash includes physical cash and demand deposits.
Cash equivalents must be shortterm, liquid and lowrisk.
Components must be disclosed.

title: 6.4.2 Classification requirement
definition: IAS 7 requires cash flows to be classified as operating, investing or financing.
overview: This classification helps users understand whether cash came from core operations, longterm asset decisions or capitalstructure changes. It applies to every cash flow reported in the statement. The classification supports comparability across companies using IFRS.
highlights: Every cash flow must be classified.
The three categories are operating, investing and financing.
Classification supports analysis of cash generation and use.

IFRS gives companies policy choices for interest and dividends: interest and dividends received are classified as operating or investing, and interest and dividends paid as operating or financing, applied consistently (as listed in an eCampusOntario IFRS text; confirm against the current standard).

title: 6.4.3 Direct method under IAS 7
definition: Under IAS 7, the direct method discloses major classes of gross cash receipts and gross cash payments.
overview: This approach presents operating cash flows directly, such as cash received from customers and cash paid to suppliers or employees. It provides a clear view of the sources and uses of operating cash. IAS 7 permits this method alongside the indirect method.
highlights: It shows gross operating cash receipts and payments.
It presents operating cash flows directly.
IAS 7 permits its use.

title: 6.4.4 Indirect method under IAS 7
definition: Under IAS 7, the indirect method adjusts profit or loss for noncash transactions, deferrals, accruals, and investing or financing income and expenses.
overview: This method begins with an accrualbased profit measure and reconciles it to operating cash flow. It is widely used because companies already maintain accrualbased income and balancesheet data. The adjustments make visible the difference between reported profit and cash generated by operations.
highlights: It starts from profit or loss.
It adjusts for noncash and timing differences.
It reconciles accrual profit to operating cash flow.

title: 6.4.5 Reconciliation to the balance sheet
definition: IAS 7 requires companies to reconcile the cash and cash equivalents in the cash flow statement with the equivalent items in the statement of financial position.
overview: This requirement creates a direct link between the closing cash balance in the cash flow statement and the balance sheet. It helps ensure that the statement explains the change in reported cash. It is a practical control for threestatement models.
highlights: Cash flow statement cash must reconcile to balancesheet cash.
The reconciliation covers cash and cash equivalents.
It supports the threestatement linkage.
The three statements together provide a fuller view of financial health than any one statement alone.
Net income becomes retained earnings on the balance sheet, adjusted for dividends.
Net income is the starting point for indirect operating cash flow.
Sales recognized on credit create accounts receivable on the balance sheet.
Operating cash flow includes cash from sales and payments for operating costs.
Investing and financing cash flows relate to assets and capital structure.

title: 6.5.1 Three-statement linkage
definition: Threestatement linkage is the set of connections through which income, balancesheet and cashflow figures affect one another.
overview: Net income from the income statement increases retained earnings, subject to dividends. It also starts the indirect operating cash flow calculation. Changes in balancesheet accounts, such as receivables, inventory, payables, PP&E, debt and equity, drive cashflow adjustments.
highlights: Net income links the income statement to equity and cash flow.
Balancesheet changes drive cashflow adjustments.
The statements must reconcile for a model to be internally consistent.

title: 6.5.2 Net income to retained earnings
definition: Net income increases retained earnings, while dividends reduce retained earnings.
overview: Investopedia states that net income at the end of a period becomes part of shareholders' equity as retained earnings. If the company pays dividends, the retainedearnings increase is smaller than net income. This link explains why a profitable company may still have limited retained earnings if it distributes much of its profit.
highlights: Retained earnings rise with profit kept in the business.
Dividends reduce retained earnings.
The link runs from the income statement to equity.

title: 6.5.3 Net income to operating cash flow
definition: Under the indirect method, net income is the starting point for calculating cash flow from operations.
overview: Investopedia explains that net income is carried to the cash flow statement as the top line for operating activities. Adjustments are then made for noncash expenses and workingcapital changes. This produces cash generated by operations rather than accounting profit alone.
highlights: Net income begins the indirect operating section.
Noncash expenses are added back.
Workingcapital changes are adjusted.

title: 6.5.4 Accounts receivable link
definition: Accounts receivable records sales made on credit that have not yet been collected in cash.
overview: Investopedia notes that sales booked during a period are added to shortterm assets as accounts receivable. Revenue can therefore rise before cash is received. When the customer later pays, accounts receivable falls and cash rises.
highlights: Credit sales create receivables.
Receivables represent cash not yet collected.
Collection converts receivables into cash.
